OVERVIEW.sub: Distributed event streaming with KRaft consensus
OVERVIEW.detail: A KRaft cluster stores all metadata in a replicated Raft log. Controllers elect a leader, the active controller commits changes, and every broker receives an immutable MetadataImage of the result.

code.label: Entry point: creates SharedServer, optional BrokerServer and ControllerServer by role

explain.body:
Apache Kafka is a system that lets applications publish and subscribe to streams of records — like a durable, distributed message queue. Thousands of companies use it for real-time data pipelines: one program writes events ("user clicked", "order placed") and others read them, at scale.

Kafka runs as a *cluster* — a group of machines called *brokers* that store and serve data. The cluster needs agreement on who owns which data: which broker holds which partition, who is alive, what configuration is active. That agreement is *metadata*.

In KRaft mode (Kafka Raft), metadata lives in a replicated log managed by *controllers* using the Raft consensus protocol. One controller wins an election and becomes the *active controller*: it alone writes metadata records. Every other node — brokers and standby controllers — replays those records to build an identical *metadata image*, an immutable snapshot of the cluster's state.

Before any of this runs, each node's storage must be formatted with `kafka-storage format`, which writes a bootstrap snapshot seeding the log with initial records.

AUTHORED.sub: Format directories and write bootstrap metadata

group.note: CLI dispatches to the Formatter, which uses Bootstrap, SCRAM, and Feature definitions

AUTHORED.detail: `kafka-storage format` writes `meta.properties` and a bootstrap snapshot into each log directory. The snapshot seeds the metadata log with `FeatureLevelRecord`s and optional SCRAM credentials.

explain.body:
Before a Kafka node can start, its storage directories must be *formatted* — stamped with a cluster identity and seeded with initial metadata. This is done once per node by running `kafka-storage format`.

Formatting writes two things to each directory: a `meta.properties` file identifying the cluster and node, and (for controllers) a *bootstrap snapshot* — a small file containing the initial metadata records. These records set the cluster's *metadata version* (the protocol version all nodes agree on) and the levels of other features like `kraft.version`.

If you skip this step, the node has no identity and no metadata log to read, so it cannot join the cluster.

explain.body:
The `Formatter` class is where the actual disk writes happen. It takes a cluster ID, node ID, metadata version, feature levels, and a list of directories, then stamps each one.

First it computes the *effective* metadata version — defaulting to the latest production version if none is specified. Then it fills in defaults for every other feature (kraft.version, group.version, etc.) based on that metadata version, validates that all cross-feature dependencies are satisfied, and assembles the *bootstrap metadata* records.

Finally it walks each empty directory, writes a `meta.properties` file with the cluster and node identity, and for metadata directories writes a bootstrap snapshot containing the records.

explain.body:
When a KRaft controller starts for the first time, its metadata log is empty. The *bootstrap metadata* provides the initial records to populate it — primarily `FeatureLevelRecord` messages that set the cluster's metadata version and other feature levels.

`BootstrapMetadata` is an immutable container for these records. It can be built from a version string (the usual path during formatting), loaded from a binary checkpoint file on disk, or assembled from a raw list of records. Every instance must contain a `FeatureLevelRecord` for `metadata.version`.

children.title: SCRAM Credentials
children.sub: Parse --add-scram into bootstrap records
children.detail: `ScramParser` turns `--add-scram` arguments like `SCRAM-SHA-256=[name=alice,password=secret]` into `UserScramCredentialRecord` messages with computed salt, storedKey, and serverKey.

explain.body:
SCRAM is a password-based authentication mechanism. When formatting a new cluster, an operator can pre-load user credentials so that authentication works from the very first start.

`ScramParser` takes arguments like `SCRAM-SHA-256=[name=alice,password=secret]`, splits the mechanism name from the config string, then parses key-value pairs for name, password (or saltedpassword), salt, and iterations. It computes the cryptographic keys — *salt* (random bytes), *storedKey* and *serverKey* (derived from the salted password) — and produces a `UserScramCredentialRecord` that goes into the bootstrap snapshot.

Iterations default to 4096 if not specified, and must stay within the mechanism's allowed range.

rows.title: Generate credential record

children.detail: The `Feature` enum registers each cluster feature (e.g., `KRaftVersion`, `TransactionVersion`) with its `FeatureVersion[]` variants and latest production level. explain.body:
Kafka's cluster features — metadata version, KRaft version, group version, and others — each have a numbered level that determines which protocol capabilities are active. Features can depend on each other: for example, `kraft.version=1` requires `metadata.version` at least `IBP_3_9_IV0`.

During formatting, the tool picks a default level for every feature based on the chosen metadata version, then validates that all dependencies are satisfied. The `FeatureVersion` interface defines the contract every feature version must follow: a level, a name, a bootstrap metadata version, and a dependency map.

explain.body:
The `Feature` enum is a central registry of every versioned capability in the cluster. Each entry holds the feature's name, its array of version objects, and the latest version considered production-ready.

When the formatter needs a default level for `group.version`, it calls `Feature.GROUP_VERSION.defaultLevel(metadataVersion)`, which walks the version array and returns the highest one whose bootstrap metadata version is at or below the given metadata version. The `validateVersion` method then checks that every dependency declared by a feature version is met in the final set.

children.detail: `MetadataVersion` is an enum of 28 versions from `IBP_3_3_IV3` (level 7) to `IBP_4_5_IV0` (level 34). `LATEST_PRODUCTION` is `IBP_4_4_IV2` (level 33).

explain.body:
The *metadata version* is the most important feature level in a Kafka cluster. It determines which record formats are used in the metadata log, which RPCs are available, and which capabilities (SCRAM, delegation tokens, tiered storage) are enabled.

It is an enum with one constant per internal version, like `IBP_3_5_IV2` (level 11, enables SCRAM) or `IBP_4_0_IV1` (level 23, enables eligible leader replicas). `LATEST_PRODUCTION` is the highest stable version; anything beyond it is testing-only and requires the unstable feature flag.

children.title: KRaft Version
children.sub: Consensus protocol version levels
children.detail: `KRaftVersion` has two levels: 0 (initial KRaft) and 1 (KIP-853 dynamic quorum). Version 1 enables reconfiguration and requires `IBP_3_9_IV0` as its bootstrap metadata version.

explain.body:
The KRaft version controls the consensus protocol between controllers. Version 0 is the original fixed-membership protocol where every controller's address is listed in a static config (`controller.quorum.voters`). Version 1 enables KIP-853 dynamic quorums, where controllers can be added and removed at runtime using `controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers` instead.

During formatting, if the operator uses `--standalone` or `--initial-controllers`, the formatter sets `kraft.version` to 1 automatically. If the static `controller.quorum.voters` config is set, it stays at 0.

AUTHORED.title: Starting a Node
AUTHORED.sub: Boot broker and controller processes in KRaft mode
AUTHORED.detail: `KafkaRaftServer` reads `process.roles` and creates a `SharedServer` plus optional `BrokerServer` and `ControllerServer`. The controller starts first so its endpoints reach the Raft manager; the broker shuts down first so controlled shutdown can complete.

explain.body:
A Kafka cluster in KRaft mode has no ZooKeeper. Every node is a single OS process that can act as a *broker* (stores data, serves clients), a *controller* (manages cluster metadata via Raft), or both at once — called *combined mode*.

When the process starts, `KafkaRaftServer` checks the `process.roles` config to decide which components to create. A `SharedServer` holds the parts both roles need: the Raft manager, the metadata loader, and the snapshot generator. The controller and broker each take a reference to it and call `startForController` or `startForBroker`; the shared server only truly starts on the first call and only truly stops when both have released it.

The startup order matters: the controller must start before the broker so the Raft manager receives the controller's listener endpoints. Shutdown is the reverse: broker first, so the controller can approve its controlled shutdown.

children.sub: Reference-counted Raft, loader, and snapshot components
children.detail: `SharedServer` is started by whichever role calls first and stopped only when both release it. It creates `KafkaRaftManager`, `MetadataLoader`, `SnapshotEmitter`, and `SnapshotGenerator`, then registers the loader with the Raft client.

explain.body:
Both the broker and the controller need the same Raft log, the same metadata loader, and the same snapshot machinery. Rather than duplicate them, `SharedServer` holds one copy and tracks who is using it with two booleans: `usedByBroker` and `usedByController`.

The first caller to `startForBroker` or `startForController` triggers the real `start()`, which builds the Raft manager, connects it to a metadata loader, and wires up snapshot generation. The last caller to `stopForBroker` or `stopForController` triggers `stop()`, which tears everything down in reverse. This design means a combined-mode node creates only one Raft manager even though two roles share it.

explain.body:
The controller is the node that manages cluster metadata: it decides which broker holds which partition, stores ACLs and quotas, and tracks broker registrations. Its startup is a long sequence of wiring.

First it opens a network socket so other nodes can reach it. Then it builds the `QuorumController`, the central state machine that processes metadata changes proposed through Raft. It loads policy plugins like `CreateTopicPolicy` and connects an authorizer. Finally it installs many *metadata publishers* — small objects that each watch the metadata log and push updates to a specific subsystem (the metadata cache, quotas, SCRAM credentials, delegation tokens, ACLs, and so on). Request processing is not enabled until the authorizer is ready and the socket server's acceptors have started.

explain.body:
The broker is the part of Kafka that stores topic partitions and serves produce/fetch requests from clients. Its startup is the longest sequence in the codebase because it must wire together many subsystems.

After calling `startForBroker()` on the shared server, it creates a log manager (which manages data directories and log segments), a replica manager (which handles replication of partitions), and several coordinators for consumer groups, transactions, and share groups. It also creates `KafkaApis`, the request processor that routes every client API call.

Before the broker opens its ports, it must catch up on the cluster's metadata: it waits for the `BrokerLifecycleManager` to report that the active controller has acknowledged it as caught up, and for the first metadata image to be published. Only then does it unfence itself and accept connections.

AUTHORED.sub: Run Raft elections and manage quorum state

group.note: State machine, epoch states, vote tracking, voter set management, and persistence work together but have no fixed order

AUTHORED.detail: A `QuorumState` drives transitions between six epoch states (Unattached → Prospective → Candidate → Leader → Follower/Resigned). Elections use a pre-vote phase, majority vote counting via `EpochElection`, and persist results to a local `quorum-state` file.

explain.body:
In a KRaft cluster, controllers need to agree on who is in charge. The leader is the one controller allowed to write metadata changes; everyone else follows it. If the leader disappears, the remaining controllers must pick a new one.

This is done through Raft elections. Each election round is called an *epoch* — a number that goes up every time a new vote happens. A node that wants to lead first sends *pre-votes* (non-binding) to check if it has enough support. If a majority say yes, it sends real votes in a new epoch. If a majority grant those, it becomes the leader.

The election state is saved to a local file (`quorum-state`) so a node remembers who it voted for across restarts. This prevents double-voting, which could let two leaders exist in the same epoch.

children.sub: Node with no known leader or leader endpoint
children.detail: A node enters `UnattachedState` at startup or when it learns of a higher epoch, waiting for an election timeout or a `BeginQuorumEpoch`. Observers stay here with `MAX_VALUE` timeout.

explain.body:
When a node starts up or loses contact with the leader, it enters the *unattached* state. It knows which epoch it is in, and may remember who it voted for, but it does not know who the current leader is or how to reach them.

The node sets an election timer. If the timer fires before it hears from a leader, it moves to the Prospective state and starts a pre-vote round. Observers — nodes that are not voters — set their timeout to infinity, so they never start elections.

explain.body:
Before a node actually asks for votes (which increments the epoch and can disrupt the cluster), it runs a *pre-vote* round. The node asks every voter: "Would you vote for me if I started a real election?" This is non-binding — nobody's state changes.

If a majority say yes, the node has confidence it can win and moves to the Candidate state. If the pre-vote fails or times out, the node falls back to Unattached (if it has no leader) or Follower (if it remembers the leader). This prevents unnecessary epoch bumps from nodes that are partitioned from the leader but can still reach voters.

children.title: Candidate State
children.sub: Requesting real votes in a new epoch

explain.body:
A candidate has passed pre-voting and now runs the real election. It increments the epoch number by one and records a vote for itself. It then asks every other voter for a binding vote.

Unlike pre-votes, a granted standard vote is persisted — the voter commits to this candidate for the epoch and cannot vote for anyone else. If the candidate gets a majority, it becomes the leader. If it gets enough rejections that a majority is impossible, or the timer expires, it falls back to Prospective for another try.

children.title: Leader State
children.sub: Elected leader tracking voters and high watermark
children.detail: `LeaderState` tracks each voter's fetch offset, computes high watermark as the median offset, runs a check-quorum timer, and appends a LeaderChange control record at epoch start.

explain.body:
Once a candidate wins the election, it becomes the leader. The leader's first action is to write a *LeaderChange* record to the Raft log, announcing who won and who voted for them. Until a majority of voters fetch past this record, the leader cannot advance the *high watermark* — the offset that is considered committed.

The leader also runs a *check-quorum* timer. If a majority of voters fail to fetch within 1.5× the fetch timeout, the leader assumes it is partitioned and steps down. This prevents a leader that has lost connectivity from accepting writes that cannot be replicated.

children.title: High Watermark
children.sub: Committed offset computed from voter fetch offsets
children.detail: The leader sorts voters by descending fetch offset and picks the median (index `size/2`). It only advances past `epochStartOffset` so the leader commits its own epoch first.

explain.body:
The high watermark is the highest offset that a majority of voters have replicated. The leader finds it by sorting all voters' fetch offsets from highest to lowest and picking the middle one — the one at position voters/2. This guarantees a majority has at least that offset.

There is an extra rule: the watermark cannot advance past the start of the current epoch until the leader's own records are replicated. This ensures the leader's epoch is committed before any older data is declared safe.

If the timer expires without a majority fetching, the leader knows it is partitioned and steps down, allowing the remaining voters to elect a new leader.

children.title: Voter Changes
children.sub: Add, remove, and update voters at runtime

explain.body:
KIP-853 lets a running cluster add or remove voters without stopping. Each change follows a careful protocol: the leader checks that the previous voter change has committed (high watermark past its offset), sends an `API_VERSIONS` request to the new voter to confirm compatibility, then writes a new VotersRecord to the log.

Only one voter change can be in flight at a time. If the leader removes itself, it resigns after the change commits. This ensures the new voter set has an overlapping majority with the old set, so no committed data is lost.

The response to the caller can be sent immediately on append or delayed until the record commits, controlled by the `ackWhenCommitted` flag.

children.sub: Fetching from the known leader
children.detail: `FollowerState` tracks the leader's id and endpoints, a fetch timer, and high watermark updates. It grants pre-votes only if it hasn't yet fetched from the leader.

explain.body:
A follower knows who the leader is and fetches records from it. Each successful fetch resets a timer; if the timer expires (no fetch succeeded within `fetchTimeoutMs`), the follower transitions to Prospective and starts a pre-vote round.

Followers are cautious about voting: they reject all standard votes (they already have a leader) and only grant pre-votes if they have not yet successfully fetched from the leader. This prevents a partitioned node from disrupting a healthy cluster.

When a leader shuts down gracefully, it does not just disappear — it resigns. It sends an `EndQuorumEpoch` request to every voter, telling them to start a new election. The resigned leader tracks which voters have acknowledged, to avoid retrying unnecessarily.

A node also starts in this state if it was the leader when it last shut down. This prevents it from accidentally acting as leader before it discovers what happened while it was offline. Once its election timer expires, it transitions to Unattached and can participate in elections again.

children.title: Election Persistence
children.sub: Saving election state to the quorum-state file
children.detail: `FileQuorumStateStore` persists `ElectionState` (epoch, leader id, voted key) as JSON to a local `quorum-state` file. Writes are atomic via temp-file-then-rename with fsync.

explain.body:
Every time a node votes or discovers a new leader, that fact must survive a crash. Otherwise the node might vote twice in the same epoch after restarting, which could allow two leaders.

The election state — epoch number, who the node voted for, who the leader is — is written to a file called `quorum-state` in JSON format. The write is atomic: the node writes to a temporary file, syncs it to disk, and renames it over the real file. This means the file is never half-written.

The write path is designed to be crash-safe: it writes to a temporary file, calls fsync to ensure the data reaches disk, and then atomically renames it over the real file.

children.title: Voter Set Management
children.sub: Immutable voter collections with overlap guarantees
children.detail: `VoterSet` is an immutable map of voter id to `VoterNode`. Add/remove return a new set, and `hasOverlappingMajority` ensures consecutive sets share a quorum.

explain.body:
The voter set is the list of nodes allowed to vote and serve as leader. It is immutable — adding or removing a voter returns a new copy. This is important because the Raft protocol relies on consecutive voter sets sharing an *overlapping majority*: any majority of the old set and any majority of the new set must have at least one member in common.

This guarantee means a committed record cannot be lost during a voter change, because at least one voter in the new set has it. The `VoterSetHistory` tracks voter sets at each log offset, so the system always knows which voters were active at any point in the log.

explain.body: Each mutation on a VoterSet returns a new copy, or empty if the precondition fails (adding a duplicate, removing the last voter). The overlap check ensures that the difference between any two consecutive voter sets is at most one member in each direction, which guarantees that any majority of one set intersects any majority of the other.

AUTHORED.title: Raft Log and Snapshots
AUTHORED.sub: Store, batch, replicate, and snapshot metadata records
AUTHORED.detail: The Raft log stores metadata as an append-only sequence of batches, with snapshots compacting older state. `KafkaRaftLog` implements the `RaftLog` interface, while `BatchAccumulator` collects records and `KafkaNetworkChannel` transports requests.

explain.body:
In a KRaft cluster, every piece of cluster metadata — topics, partitions, broker registrations — is stored as a record in the *metadata log*. This log is an append-only sequence: new records go on the end and are never changed.

Over time the log grows, so periodically a *snapshot* is taken: a file that captures the full state at a given offset. Once a snapshot exists, older log segments can be deleted. Every controller and broker keeps its own copy of this log and its snapshots.

Before records reach the log they are collected into *batches* by the `BatchAccumulator`. A batch groups several records together so they can be written and replicated efficiently. The network transport layer sends these batches — and other Raft protocol messages — between nodes.

children.title: The Metadata Log
children.sub: Append-only log of metadata record batches
children.detail: `RaftLog` defines the contract for appending, reading, truncating, and managing high watermark. `KafkaRaftLog` implements it over a `UnifiedLog` and a `TreeMap` of snapshots, with `MetadataLogConfig` controlling segment and retention sizes.

explain.body:
The metadata log is an ordered, append-only sequence of record batches stored on disk. A leader appends records with its epoch, while a follower appends replicated records from the leader without additional validation.

Reading the log uses an *isolation level*: COMMITTED reads only up to the high watermark (the offset acknowledged by a quorum), while UNCOMMITTED reads everything. Truncation removes records from the tail, used when a follower discovers it has diverged from the leader.

The log is backed by Kafka's `UnifiedLog` (the same storage engine used for data topics), wrapped in `KafkaRaftLog` which adds snapshot tracking.

explain.body:
The `RaftLog` interface is the contract for all log operations. There are two kinds of append: `appendAsLeader` assigns the leader's epoch to records, while `appendAsFollower` accepts already-epoched records from the leader.

Reading uses an isolation level. COMMITTED returns records up to the *high watermark* — the offset that a quorum has acknowledged. UNCOMMITTED returns everything up to the end.

`validateOffsetAndEpoch` checks whether a given offset and epoch are consistent with the log. If the offset is too old, it says 'send a snapshot'; if the epoch diverges, it says where.

This is where the `RaftLog` interface meets the disk. `KafkaRaftLog` delegates all segment reads and writes to Kafka's `UnifiedLog`, the same storage engine used for data topics.

The static `createLog` factory creates a `UnifiedLog`, recovers any snapshots from the log directory, and truncates the log if a snapshot is newer than the log end — a recovery case after a crash.

children.title: Batch Accumulation
children.sub: Collect records into batches before appending
children.detail: `BatchAccumulator` collects data and control records into `CompletedBatch` objects, backed by `BatchBuilder` for serialization and `BatchMemoryPool` for buffer reuse. A linger timer triggers draining.

explain.body:
Before records are written to the metadata log, they are gathered into *batches* — groups of records that are written and replicated together. Batching reduces the overhead of each individual record.

The `BatchAccumulator` manages this. When a caller appends records, they go into a `BatchBuilder` that serializes them into Kafka's record format. When a batch is full or a linger timer expires, the batch is 'completed' and ready to drain.

Draining is the act of removing completed batches from the accumulator so they can be written to the log. A `drainOffset` mechanism allows delaying the drain of certain records — used when writing snapshot headers and footers.

children.title: Record Accumulator
children.sub: Linger timer and drain control for batching
children.detail: `BatchAccumulator` validates epoch, manages a `ConcurrentLinkedQueue` of completed batches, and supports `drainOffset` to delay draining. `appendControlMessages` force-drains before writing control records.

explain.body:
The accumulator is the entry point for all records going into the metadata log. It validates that the caller's epoch matches the current leader epoch — a stale epoch means the caller is no longer the leader.

Records go into a current batch until it's full or a linger timer fires. Completed batches sit in a queue until drained. The drain mechanism uses a three-phase protocol (NONE → STARTED → FINISHED) and respects the append lock so draining and appending can happen concurrently.

children.title: Batch Builder
children.sub: Serializes records into a single MemoryRecords batch
children.detail: `BatchBuilder` writes records using `RecordSerde` into a compressed output stream, tracks offset deltas, and finalizes with `writeDefaultBatchHeader` at `build()`. Keys are always null for metadata records.

explain.body:
A `BatchBuilder` takes individual records and serializes them into Kafka's binary record format (magic V2). Each record is written as a size-prefixed body containing a timestamp delta, offset delta, null key, serialized value, and empty headers.

When `build()` is called, the compression stream is closed and a batch header is written at the front of the buffer with the leader epoch, offset range, and record count. The result is a `MemoryRecords` ready for the log.

children.title: Buffer Pool
children.sub: Reusable fixed-size ByteBuffers for batch allocation
children.detail: `BatchMemoryPool` maintains a lock-guarded `ArrayDeque` of freed buffers up to `maxRetainedBatches`. `tryAllocate` reuses a pooled buffer or allocates a new one; `release` returns it or lets GC reclaim excess.

explain.body:
Every batch needs a ByteBuffer to hold its data. Allocating a new buffer each time is wasteful, so `BatchMemoryPool` keeps a pool of reused buffers.

When a batch finishes, its buffer is returned via `release`. If the pool has room (under `maxRetainedBatches`), the buffer is kept for the next batch. Otherwise it is discarded for garbage collection.

children.sub: Create, write, read, and clean snapshots
children.detail: `RecordsSnapshotWriter` serializes records with header/footer control batches into a `FileRawSnapshotWriter`. `RecordsSnapshotReader` decodes them with header validation.

explain.body:
A *snapshot* is a file that captures the complete cluster metadata at a particular log offset. Instead of replaying the entire log from the beginning, a node can load a snapshot and only replay records after it.

Snapshots are written to a temp file, then atomically renamed when frozen. Each snapshot starts with a header control record (containing a timestamp) and ends with a footer. Between them are the actual data records, accumulated in batches.

Old snapshots are cleaned up based on size and time retention, similar to how log segments are cleaned.

When the active controller decides to create a snapshot, it uses `RecordsSnapshotWriter`. The writer starts by appending a control batch containing a `SnapshotHeaderRecord` (with the timestamp of the last log record included). If the cluster uses KRaft version 1, a `KRaftVersionRecord` and optionally a `VotersRecord` are also added.

Data records are then appended in batches. When `freeze()` is called, a footer control record is appended, all remaining batches are drained to the raw writer, and the snapshot file is frozen.

explain.body:
When the Raft client or a snapshot reader needs to consume log records, they go through the record decoding layer. Raw bytes on disk or in memory are decoded into typed `Batch<T>` objects that the application can use.

The `RecordsIterator` handles both `MemoryRecords` (already in memory) and `FileRecords` (read from disk in chunks). A `RecordsDecodingStrategy` decides which records to decode — data records, control records, or both — allowing readers that only need metadata to skip the data.

children.title: Network Transport
children.sub: Send Raft protocol requests between nodes
children.detail: `KafkaNetworkChannel` sends requests via `KafkaClient` on a background thread. `RequestManager` tracks per-node connection state with backoff and timeout.

explain.body:
The Raft protocol requires nodes to exchange messages — vote requests, fetch requests, snapshot fetch requests, and more. The network transport layer handles this communication.

`KafkaNetworkChannel` is the entry point: it queues outbound requests to a background `SendThread` which uses Kafka's `KafkaClient` (the standard network client) to transmit them. Responses are converted back to `RaftResponse.Inbound` and delivered via `CompletableFuture`.

`RequestManager` prevents overwhelming any single node: it tracks which nodes have pending requests, enforces timeouts, and backs off after failures.

This is the bridge between the Raft protocol and Kafka's network layer. When the Raft client needs to send a vote, fetch, or snapshot request, it calls `send()`. The request is converted from an API message into the correct request builder (Vote, Fetch, FetchSnapshot, etc.), queued, and the send thread wakes up.

The response handling converts errors — version mismatches, authentication failures, disconnects — into error response messages rather than throwing exceptions, so the Raft client always gets a response.

explain.body:
The request manager prevents sending too many requests at once. Each node has a `ConnectionState` that tracks whether a request is pending, when it was sent, and whether the node is in a backoff period after a failure.

A key invariant: there can be only one pending Fetch request at a time across all connections. This prevents a follower from writing the same offset twice. The manager enforces this by checking all connections before allowing a new fetch.

AUTHORED.sub: Register brokers and controllers, then heartbeat
AUTHORED.detail: Brokers register via `BrokerLifecycleManager` (KIP-631) and heartbeat periodically; controllers self-register via `ControllerRegistrationManager` (KIP-919). Both send RPCs through a `NodeToControllerChannelManager`.

explain.body:
A Kafka cluster needs to know which brokers and controllers are alive. In KRaft mode (no ZooKeeper), every broker and controller announces itself to the active controller by sending an RPC — a remote procedure call, a structured message over the network.

A *broker* sends a `BrokerRegistrationRequest` once at startup, receives an *epoch* (a version number for this registration), then sends periodic `BrokerHeartbeatRequest` messages. The heartbeat tells the controller the broker's metadata offset, whether it wants to be fenced or shut down, and which log directories are offline. The controller replies with flags like `isCaughtUp` and `shouldShutDown` that drive the broker's state machine.

A *controller* sends a `ControllerRegistrationRequest` once its metadata version is high enough (3.7+, KIP-919). It watches the metadata log to confirm its registration was persisted, retrying with exponential backoff on failure.

explain.body:
A broker goes through a strict sequence of states. When it first starts, it sends a registration request to the active controller. Once registered, it heartbeats periodically. The controller's heartbeat reply tells it when it has caught up with metadata (STARTING→RECOVERY) and when it is unfenced (RECOVERY→RUNNING).

All state changes happen on a single event queue thread. External calls like `beginControlledShutdown()` are translated into events placed on this queue, so there are no race conditions between state transitions.

If the controller responds with success, the broker stores the assigned *epoch* — a version number the controller increments each time this broker registers. All future heartbeats include this epoch. If registration fails, the broker retries after a heartbeat interval. If it never succeeds within `initialRegistrationTimeoutMs`, the broker shuts down.

After registering, the broker sends a heartbeat on a timer (default every few seconds). The heartbeat carries the broker's current metadata offset so the controller knows how far behind it is, plus flags: `wantFence` is true until the broker is ready to serve clients, and `wantShutDown` is true during controlled shutdown.

The controller replies with `isCaughtUp`, `isFenced`, and `shouldShutDown`. These flags drive the broker's state machine forward — from STARTING to RECOVERY when caught up, from RECOVERY to RUNNING when unfenced, and from PENDING_CONTROLLED_SHUTDOWN to SHUTTING_DOWN when the controller says to go.

When an operator stops a broker gracefully, the broker does not just disappear. It enters PENDING_CONTROLLED_SHUTDOWN and starts sending heartbeats with `wantShutDown=true`. The controller uses this time to move partition leaders off the broker.

Once the controller is satisfied that the broker can leave safely, it replies with `shouldShutDown=true`. The broker then transitions to SHUTTING_DOWN, closes its channel, and completes the `controlledShutdownFuture`. If the broker was not in RUNNING state when shutdown was requested, it skips the controlled phase and shuts down immediately.

In older Kafka, controllers did not register themselves — they were simply the nodes that won the Raft election. KIP-919 added explicit controller registration so the cluster metadata records which controllers exist and what features they support.

The `ControllerRegistrationManager` implements `MetadataPublisher`, meaning it receives metadata updates. It watches for two things: whether the metadata version is high enough to support registration, and whether its own registration has appeared in the log. If not registered and conditions are met, it sends a `ControllerRegistrationRequest`. On failure it retries with exponential backoff (100ms base, 120s max).

If the controller changes (a `NOT_CONTROLLER` error) or the connection drops, the thread disconnects, clears its cached controller address, and re-queries the `RaftControllerNodeProvider` on the next poll. `BrokerState` is the enum whose values appear in metrics and on the wire. `BrokerHeartbeatReply` and `BrokerRegistrationReply` are small records the controller returns. `ListenerInfo` handles the ordered map of listener endpoints with factory methods for each RPC and record format.

AUTHORED.title: Active Controller
AUTHORED.sub: Validate and commit metadata for the cluster
AUTHORED.detail: `QuorumController` is single-threaded: every write generates records, replays them in-memory, then appends to the Raft log. The future completes only when the log commits.

explain.body:
In a KRaft cluster, one controller node is the *active controller* — the Raft leader for the metadata log. Every change to the cluster (creating a topic, registering a broker, updating a config) must go through this one node.

The active controller validates the request, produces metadata *records* describing the change, applies them to its own in-memory state, and hands them to the Raft layer for replication. The caller's future does not complete until the records are committed by a majority of voters. If the controller loses leadership, it *renounces* — reverts to the last committed state and fails all pending operations.

Standby controllers replay committed records but cannot generate new ones. This single-writer design avoids locking: one thread processes every event in order.

group.note: Sub-managers handle independent domains; the event queue and replay tie them together

children.title: Event Queue
children.sub: Single-threaded queue executing reads and writes
children.detail: All controller operations are events on a `KafkaEventQueue`. Writes generate records via `ControllerWriteOperation`, replay them, append to Raft, then park in the deferred queue until committed.

explain.body:
The controller processes every request on a single thread — no locks, no races. An API call like `createTopics` creates a *write event* and puts it on a queue. When the event runs, it calls the relevant sub-manager to produce metadata records.

Those records are immediately applied to in-memory state (so the next event sees them) and handed to the Raft layer. But the caller's future does not complete yet — it is parked in a *deferred event queue* until Raft reports the records are committed by a majority. A read event works similarly but generates no records.

children.title: Write Event Processing
children.sub: Generate records, replay, and append to Raft
children.detail: `ControllerWriteEvent.run()` checks the controller is active, calls `generateRecordsAndResult()`, replays each record in-memory, then calls `raftClient.prepareAppend` and `schedulePreparedAppend`.

explain.body:
When a write event reaches the front of the queue, it first checks that this controller is still the Raft leader (the *active controller*). If not, it throws `NotControllerException` and the caller must retry against the real leader.

If active, it calls the sub-manager's `generateRecordsAndResult` to produce metadata records. Each record is immediately applied to in-memory state via `replay()`. Then the batch is handed to Raft for replication. If the batch has no records (a no-op write), it either completes immediately or waits for any pending purgatory items.

explain.body: After a write event appends records to the Raft log, its future is parked in a *deferred event queue* keyed by the log offset those records were written at. The Raft layer calls `handleCommit` each time new batches are committed. The active controller then advances the committed offset and calls `completeUpTo`, which finds every parked future at or below the new stable offset and completes it. This is how callers learn their write is durable.

children.title: Claiming Leadership
children.sub: Transition between active and standby
children.detail: When Raft elects this node leader, `claim()` sets the epoch and activates sub-managers. `renounce()` reverts to last committed state, fails pending operations, and deactivates.

explain.body:
A controller node is either *active* (the Raft leader, allowed to write) or *standby* (a follower, read-only). The Raft layer notifies the controller of leadership changes through `handleLeaderChange`.

When this node becomes leader, `claim()` sets `curClaimEpoch` to the new epoch and activates the heartbeat manager and other sub-managers. It then prepends a *complete activation* event that writes bootstrap records (on a fresh cluster) or aborts any in-flight transaction left by the previous leader.

When leadership is lost, `renounce()` resets the epoch to -1, resigns from Raft, fails all deferred operations, and deactivates sub-managers. The in-memory state reverts to the last committed snapshot.

children.title: Topics and Partitions
children.sub: Create, delete, reassign topics and elect leaders
children.detail: `ReplicationControlManager` owns topic/partition state: creation via `StripedReplicaPlacer`, deletion, ISR changes via `alterPartition`, leader election, and broker fencing effects on partitions.

explain.body:
Topics and their partitions are the core data the controller manages. When someone creates a topic, the controller must decide which brokers hold each partition's replicas — this is *replica placement*. When a broker reports its ISR has changed, the controller validates and records the new ISR. When a broker is fenced or shuts down, the controller must elect new partition leaders.

All of this lives in `ReplicationControlManager`, the largest sub-manager. It tracks every topic and partition in timeline hash maps, and uses helper structures like `BrokersToIsrs` to quickly find all partitions affected by a broker going away.

children.sub: Register brokers and controllers, manage heartbeats
children.detail: `ClusterControlManager` handles broker and controller registration, validates features and directories, and owns the `BrokerHeartbeatManager` that tracks sessions and decides broker state transitions.

explain.body:
Before a broker can serve traffic it must *register* with the active controller, sending its listeners, feature versions, and log directories. The controller validates this against finalized features and records it as a `RegisterBrokerRecord`. The broker then heartbeats periodically.

The `BrokerHeartbeatManager` decides each broker's next state: FENCED (just registered or lost contact), UNFENCED (caught up and healthy), CONTROLLED_SHUTDOWN (draining leaders), or SHUTDOWN_NOW (safe to stop). A periodic task fences brokers whose heartbeat session has expired.

The controller checks the cluster ID matches, every finalized feature is supported by the broker, and no log directory belongs to another broker. Each broker heartbeat carries the broker's current metadata offset and flags for wanting to shut down or fence. The heartbeat manager uses these to decide the broker's next state:

- A *fenced* broker becomes *unfenced* once its metadata offset reaches its registration record offset (it has caught up).
- An *unfenced* broker requesting shutdown enters *controlled shutdown* if it leads partitions, so leaders can be moved first.
- A *controlled shutdown* broker gets *shutdown now* once all its leaders are moved and its shutdown offset is below the lowest active broker offset.

AUTHORED.title: The Metadata Image
AUTHORED.sub: Immutable snapshots and deltas of cluster state
AUTHORED.detail: `MetadataImage` is an immutable record of nine domain images—topics, cluster, features, ACLs, configs, quotas, SCRAM, tokens, producer IDs—stamped with a `MetadataProvenance`. `MetadataDelta` accumulates replayed records and applies them to produce the next image.

explain.body:
A Kafka cluster's *metadata* is everything the brokers and controllers need to agree on: which topics exist, where their partitions live, who is allowed to do what, and what configuration is active. All of this state must be the same on every node.

The metadata image is a complete, frozen picture of that state at one point in time. It is a Java record that holds smaller, per-domain images—one for topics, one for cluster registrations, one for ACLs, and so on. Because it is immutable, any thread can read it without locking.

To move to a newer picture, the system replays committed log records into a *delta*—a mutable accumulator that tracks what changed in each domain. When all records are replayed, `apply()` produces a new image, and the old one can be discarded.

children.title: Topics And Partitions
children.sub: Topic images, deltas, and per-broker replica changes

group.note: Three aspects of topic metadata: the immutable images, the delta tracking, and the per-broker view

children.detail: `TopicsImage` indexes topics by UUID and name using persistent immutable maps. `TopicsDelta` tracks creations, deletions, and partition changes, and `localChanges()` extracts the per-broker view.

explain.body:
Topics are the richest domain in the metadata image. Each topic has a name, a UUID, and a map of partitions. Each partition records its replicas, ISR (in-sync replicas), leader, and epochs.

The topics image uses persistent immutable maps, so adding or removing a topic produces a new map that shares most of its structure with the old one, rather than copying everything.

The delta tracks three things: changed topics (created or modified partitions), deleted topic IDs, and newly created topics. When applied, deletions are processed first, then additions and updates.

AUTHORED.title: Propagating Metadata
AUTHORED.sub: Load committed records and publish to brokers
AUTHORED.detail: MetadataLoader follows the Raft log, packages committed records into deltas and images, and fans each update out to MetadataPublisher plugins such as KRaftMetadataCachePublisher, AclPublisher, and DynamicClientQuotaPublisher.

explain.body:
In a KRaft cluster, every piece of cluster metadata — topics, ACLs, quotas, configurations — is stored as records in a single Raft log called `__cluster_metadata`. The active controller writes to this log; every other node needs to read it and keep its own state up to date.

That is what this subsystem does. A component called the *MetadataLoader* watches the Raft log for new commits. It replays each record into a *delta* (a set of changes) and produces a new *metadata image* (the full state after those changes). It then calls every registered *publisher* — a plugin that cares about some slice of metadata — handing each one the delta and the new image.

Publishers include the broker's metadata cache (so it can answer client requests), the ACL authorizer (so it can enforce permissions), quota managers, SCRAM credential providers, and the broker's own replica manager. The loader guarantees ordering: publishers see updates in log order, and a new publisher gets a full snapshot before it sees any deltas.

explain.body:
The MetadataLoader is the bridge between the Raft consensus layer and the rest of the broker. It listens for two kinds of events: committed batches (normal log appends) and snapshot loads (when the node fell too far behind and must load a full snapshot instead).

Before the loader publishes anything, it waits until it has caught up with the Raft high water mark. This prevents publishers from seeing a partial view of the cluster. Once caught up, every commit is packaged into a delta and image and delivered to all publishers in installation order.

When a new publisher is installed after startup, the loader creates a synthetic snapshot delta from the empty image to the current image and delivers that first, so the publisher starts with a consistent full picture.

The StandardAuthorizer is Kafka's built-in access control system. It checks whether a request is allowed by scanning ACLs that match the requested resource. ACLs are stored in an immutable sorted set, indexed by resource type and name.

Authorization works in layers: super-users (configured via `super.users`) are always allowed. If loading is not yet complete, any non-super-user request throws an exception. Once loaded, the authorizer scans matching ACLs: any DENY match immediately denies; otherwise an ALLOW match permits. If no ACLs match, a configurable default (usually DENY) applies.

children.sub: Quotas, SCRAM, tokens, and features

group.note: Each handles one independent metadata domain

children.detail: Several small publishers each handle one domain: `FeaturesPublisher` tracks finalized features, `ScramPublisher` updates credentials, `DelegationTokenPublisher` syncs tokens, and `DynamicClientQuotaPublisher` passes quota deltas.

explain.body:
Beyond topics and ACLs, the metadata log carries many other kinds of cluster state. Each is handled by a small, focused publisher that implements the MetadataPublisher interface. They check if their relevant delta is present, apply changes to their component, and catch exceptions via a fault handler.

For example, ScramPublisher watches for SCRAM credential changes and updates the credential provider so authentication stays current. FeaturesPublisher keeps a volatile snapshot of finalized features.

explain.body: SCRAM is a password authentication mechanism. The ScramPublisher watches for credential changes in the metadata log and applies them to the broker's CredentialProvider so that authentication stays in sync with the controller's state.

explain.body: Client quotas limit how much bandwidth or request rate each client can use. The DynamicClientQuotaPublisher simply checks if there is a client quotas delta and, if so, passes it to the quota updater callback which applies the changes to the broker's quota manager.

children.title: Snapshot Generation
children.sub: Emit KRaft snapshots on thresholds
children.detail: SnapshotGenerator is a MetadataPublisher that tracks bytes and time since the last snapshot. When a threshold is met and the offset is batch-aligned, it schedules SnapshotEmitter to write the image.

explain.body:
As the metadata log grows, nodes that fall behind would need to replay a huge number of records. Snapshots solve this: a snapshot is a complete picture of the metadata at a given offset. A node that needs to catch up can load the latest snapshot instead of replaying the entire log.

The SnapshotGenerator watches every metadata update. If enough bytes (default 100 MB) or time (default 1 day) have passed, and the current image is batch-aligned, it schedules the SnapshotEmitter to write the image to disk in batches of 1024 records.

children.title: Threshold Check
children.sub: Decide when to snapshot
children.detail: Counts bytes since last snapshot and time elapsed. If either exceeds the configured maximum and the event queue is empty, schedules an emit if the offset is batch-aligned and snapshotting is not disabled.

explain.body: Each log delta adds its byte count to a running total. If the total exceeds 100 MB or more than a day has passed since the last snapshot, the generator considers emitting. It checks that the event queue is empty (so it doesn't pile up), that the offset is batch-aligned, and that snapshots aren't disabled (which happens during shutdown).

rows.detail: Adds manifest.numBytes() to bytesSinceLastSnapshot.

rows.title: Check byte threshold
rows.detail: If bytes >= maxBytesSinceLastSnapshot and queue empty, try to schedule.

rows.title: Check time threshold
rows.detail: If elapsed >= maxTimeSinceLastSnapshotNs and queue empty, try to schedule.

rows.title: Guard and schedule
rows.detail: Skips if disabled or not batch-aligned; otherwise enqueues emitter.maybeEmit.

children.detail: Creates a `SnapshotWriter` via `raftClient.createSnapshot`, writes the image in batches of 1024 records using `RaftSnapshotWriter`, and updates byte/time metrics on success.

explain.body: The SnapshotEmitter is the component that actually writes the snapshot file. It asks the Raft client to create a snapshot writer for the image's offset and epoch. If one already exists, it skips. Otherwise, it serialises the entire metadata image into the writer in batches and finalises it.

AUTHORED.title: Inspecting the Cluster
AUTHORED.sub: Query cluster state from command-line tools
AUTHORED.detail: Three CLI tools — `kafka-cluster`, `kafka-features`, `kafka-metadata-quorum` — query and mutate cluster state via the Admin API. A tree of `MetadataNode` classes lets internal code walk the metadata image for debugging.

explain.body:
Once a KRaft cluster is running, operators need to check its health and manage its features from the command line. Kafka ships three shell commands for this.

`kafka-cluster` shows the cluster ID, lists broker and controller endpoints, and can unregister a node. `kafka-features` describes, upgrades, or downgrades feature flags like `metadata.version` and `kraft.version`. `kafka-metadata-quorum` shows quorum status (who is leader, how far behind followers are) and can add or remove controllers from the voter set.

Behind these tools, the metadata image — an immutable snapshot of all cluster state — can also be walked as a tree of nodes for programmatic inspection, with sensitive fields redacted.

explain.body:
Kafka's behaviour is controlled by *feature flags* like `metadata.version` and `kraft.version`. Each flag has a numeric level that the cluster has *finalized* (agreed on). Upgrading a flag unlocks new capabilities; downgrading it (sometimes destructively) reverts them.

`kafka-features describe` shows every flag's supported range and finalized level. `upgrade` and `downgrade` change flag levels, either one at a time or all at once with `--release-version`. `disable` sets a flag to level 0. `version-mapping` and `feature-dependencies` are local lookups that don't contact the cluster.

The metadata image is a large, immutable snapshot of everything the cluster knows: topics, brokers, configs, ACLs, and more. To let tools and debuggers explore it without knowing its internals, it is wrapped in a tree of `MetadataNode` objects. Each node has a name, can list its children, and can look up a child by name — like a file system.

The root node, `MetadataImageNode`, delegates to ten child domains (topics, cluster, features, configs, etc.). Leaf nodes print their values through a `MetadataNodePrinter`, which can redact sensitive data like passwords and SCRAM keys.

rows.detail: Parses records by ControlRecordType: LEADER_CHANGE, SNAPSHOT_HEADER, SNAPSHOT_FOOTER, KRAFT_VERSION, KRAFT_VOTERS.

rows.title: Parse data batch
rows.detail: Deserializes each record with `MetadataRecordSerde.INSTANCE.read()`.

children.title: Batch File Writer
children.sub: Write metadata records in snapshot format
children.detail: `BatchFileWriter` wraps a `BatchAccumulator` and `FileChannel`. `open()` writes a `SnapshotHeaderRecord`; `close()` writes a `SnapshotFooterRecord` and drains all batches to disk.

explain.body: This class creates a new file in the same binary format as a KRaft snapshot. It starts with a snapshot header record, accumulates metadata records into batches, and on close writes a footer record and flushes everything to disk. Tools use it to create snapshot files for offline inspection or testing.

code.label: Full writer: open with header, append, close with footer

rows.title: Open with header
rows.detail: Creates BatchAccumulator, appends SnapshotHeaderRecord, drains the header batch.

rows.title: Append records
rows.detail: Callers add records or batches via `batchAccumulator.append()`.

rows.title: Close with footer
rows.detail: Appends SnapshotFooterRecord, force-drains, writes all completed batches to FileChannel.

children.title: Snapshot File Reader
children.sub: Replay a snapshot file through a Raft listener
children.detail: `SnapshotFileReader` opens a snapshot file and processes batches asynchronously via `KafkaEventQueue`. Control batches trigger `listener.handleLeaderChange()`; data batches trigger `listener.handleCommit()`.

explain.body: Unlike `BatchFileReader` which just iterates, this class replays a snapshot file as if a live Raft node were receiving the data. It uses an event queue to process batches asynchronously, calling the same listener methods (`handleLeaderChange`, `handleCommit`) that a running broker or controller would receive. This lets tools like the metadata shell load a snapshot and build a full metadata image from it.

code.label: Full reader: startup, handleNextBatch, control/metadata handlers, close

rows.title: Startup
rows.detail: Opens FileRecords, gets batch iterator, schedules first batch processing event.

rows.title: Handle next batch
rows.detail: Pops next batch, updates high watermark on last, routes to control or metadata handler.

rows.title: Control batch
rows.detail: Parses LEADER_CHANGE and calls `listener.handleLeaderChange()`.

rows.title: Metadata batch
rows.detail: Deserializes records and calls `listener.handleCommit()` with a `MemoryBatchReader`.

rows.title: Shutdown
rows.detail: Completes the `caughtUpFuture` and closes the event queue.
